sections.h2: How to Make an AI Product Photo in 3 Simple Steps
paras: Upload a sharp photo and name the setting. Download after you check the color, with no studio day.
Upload your product photo, or describe the picture in one plain line. Keep the whole product sharp.
Rest the phone so it stays still. Use the volume button or a short timer when the shutter fires.
Fill most of the picture and leave a slim margin. Step closer instead of pinching to zoom.
Set the product beside a window in bright, indirect daylight, and turn the ceiling lights off.
Warm bulbs mixed with daylight shift the color, and that shift shows up in later images too.
A plain board, a gray card, or bare wood is enough behind the product. Wipe dust before you shoot.
Hold the phone level with the product, and keep every edge inside the picture.
Turn off portrait mode, filters, and beauty settings. They blur the background and change the color.
Tap the product to lock focus. If white areas lose all detail, lower the brightness until you see the texture.
Take a side, a three-quarter view, and any other side the listing needs. Each one needs its own photo.
Upload only a side the photo actually showed. Zoom until the edges are clear, and compare the color in daylight.
Upload the original file, not a screenshot. JPG, JPEG, PNG, WebP, BMP, TIF, TIFF, HEIC, and HEIF work. The limit is 32 MB.
Describe the scene in one sentence: the product, the surface, and the light. Save the price for your own editor.
Download and check the real product beside the screen. Fix the color or the edges with a follow-up sentence if needed.
Open a lifestyle photo, a new background, or a white background when the listing needs a different file.
The same still can start [AI image to video](page:image-to-video) when the listing also needs a short video.

Try a bright outdoor table, with the side that faced the camera.
Try a bench in early light, with the parts a shopper needs to read still easy to see.
Show a side only when your photo showed that side. Then try a three-quarter view from its own photo.
Show the product on bare wood, the whole item in frame, with a simple room behind it.
Use a plain light board, with daylight from the side, and keep the full shape in frame.
Try a low angle only at the size your photo showed.
Try a clean side view, with every edge inside the picture.
Try a desk only when the source photo showed the parts you want in frame.
Keep the color the same as the item you sell, with nothing smoothed away.
Lay the product on its side only if that side was in the source photo.
Use a front view only when the source photo showed the front.

faq.q: What does a product photo generator do?
faq.a: It makes a realistic product image from a photo you provide. You can set the background, the light, and the style without a traditional shoot.

faq.q: How does the product photo get made?
faq.a: You upload a product photo and say where it should sit. The picture comes back in that setting, and you can adjust the light and the style.

faq.q: What should I look for before I publish?
faq.a: The edges must be clear, the color must match the real item in daylight, and no side should appear that your photo never showed.

faq.q: Can I use a product photo tool for free?
faq.a: No. One image is 24 credits. Plans are on [pricing](page:pricing): Starter is $24.50 a month for 200 credits, Pro is $35 for 300, and Premium is $63 for 600. The cost shows before the job starts.

faq.q: Are these photos useful on a product page?
faq.a: Yes. A product page can use the photo, and an ad can use a second file of the same product with a different crop.

faq.q: What do I gain from an AI product photo?
faq.a: You get a new setting around the product before you rent anything. If the place looks wrong, you still have the original phone photo.

faq.q: Can I sell with these photos?
faq.a: Yes, you can use the download in your store and ads if you own or have permission to use the photo you uploaded.

faq.q: Do I need a camera, or is a phone enough?
faq.a: A phone is enough. Window light, filters off, and the whole product in the frame matter more than the camera body.
